videos.title: Project Atlas in 90 seconds
videos.summary: Why Project Atlas exists, how the twelve months run, who does the work, the five stages every item moves through and where to find things in the Atlas.

params.title: Project Atlas in 90 seconds
params.subtitle: Why we're doing it, how the year runs and where everything lives

lines.text: Ninety seconds for a whole program? I've had meetings take longer to find the dial-in.
Then let's beat them. Chip's got the stopwatch.
Over twelve months, we document, approve and launch every HR policy, process and legal obligation.
Across 13 jurisdictions? That's 438 items. And we tracked them in a spreadsheet called final_v7?
lines.say: Across thirteen jurisdictions? That's four hundred thirty-eight items. And we tracked them in a spreadsheet called final v seven?

lines.text: Which is exactly the problem. For a public company, every gap is audit or legal exposure.
Mobilize starts October 12: four weeks to set up the team, tools and approval chains.
lines.say: Mobilize starts October twelfth: four weeks to set up the team, tools and approval chains.

lines.text: Then the waves. Let me guess, scariest stuff first?
Yep. Wave 1 tackles the riskiest must-haves, Waves 2 and 3 finish every required item, and Wave 4 makes it stick.
Done by October 8, 2027. Blocking my calendar now.
lines.say: Done by October eighth, twenty twenty-seven. Blocking my calendar now.

lines.text: Who's doing all this? Please don't say me.
Six workstreams, each with a named lead. Regional and country HR leads handle the local details.
Good, because Germany doesn't exactly run like Texas.

lines.text: Every item moves through five stages: discover what exists, then draft it in the standard template.
Then review and approve, where my emails usually go to die.
Not here. Approvals run in the Atlas. Go live means published, communicated and evidence filed.

videos.title: Find and update your items
videos.summary: How to find your items in the Master checklist, take ownership, and keep status, target dates and notes current every week.

params.title: Find and update your items
params.subtitle: A few minutes a week keeps the whole program honest

lines.text: Ava, there are 438 items in the Atlas. How do I find mine?
Two filters. Open the Master checklist and I'll show you.
First, filter by wave. Let's pick Wave 1.
Then by workstream, which is my team, Talent Acquisition.
Now it's a short list. Open one, like Background screening.
Set yourself as the assignee. Type your name and pick yourself from the list.
Done. It's officially mine. No take-backs.
Now set the status to Drafting and a target date you actually believe in.
Saved for everyone, instantly. Goodbye, emailing the tracker around.

right.title: Helpful
items: Gap: no China or Taiwan addendum

lines.text: Then add a note: where the document lives, what's missing, your next step.
So not just "working on it"? That's been my status since 2019.
A good note means nobody has to chase you.

params.label: Why weekly
params.text: The status report is generated from the checklist. Update weekly and the report tells the truth.

lines.text: How often do I need to do this?
Every week. The status report is generated straight from the checklist, so leadership reads what you enter.
Skip a week and the steering committee reads old news. Got it.
Uh oh. Why is this one red?
It's overdue: the target date has passed and the item isn't finished. Maybe the approver's on vacation.
Classic. So do I just quietly move the date?
Not quietly. Note what's blocking it, agree a new date with your workstream lead, then update it.

params.title: Filter. Open. Update. Note. Every week.

params.where: Master checklist, filtered to your wave and team

lines.text: Filter, open, assign yourself, update status and date, leave a note. Every week.
A few minutes a week and nobody chases me? Sold. Next up, documenting a process.

videos.title: Document a process in five steps
videos.summary: How to turn a real process into an Atlas process document: discovery workshop, swimlane map, controls and evidence, country notes and submission for approval.

params.title: Document a process in five steps
params.subtitle: From how it really works to an approved process map

lines.text: I just inherited TA-05, background checks. Where do I start?
lines.say: I just inherited T A five, background checks. Where do I start?

lines.text: Five steps, and the first one comes with coffee.

steps.title: Workshop
steps.detail: 90 minutes with the people who do the work

steps.title: Controls
steps.detail: What's checked, by whom, with what evidence

steps.title: Country notes
steps.detail: Only where local law changes a step

lines.text: Here they are. Step one is a 90-minute workshop with the people who actually do the work.
So not just the person who wrote the procedure in 2015?
Right. Pro tip: walk one real, recent case from start to finish.
Step two: map a swimlane, one lane per role, starting with the trigger.
Tasks are boxes, and every "it depends" becomes a decision?
Exactly. Follow every branch to the end, even the awkward ones.

params.label: Watch out
params.text: Map what really happens today, not what the policy says should happen.

lines.text: Watch out for the classic trap: mapping the ideal, not what really happens.
Guilty. My last map had zero exceptions and a very happy unicorn.
If it really takes three weeks, write three weeks.

params.title: Controls and evidence
items: No check before the offer and signed consent
No adverse decision without assessment and notice
Key and SOX controls flagged for review

lines.text: Step three: controls. What gets checked, by whom, with what evidence.
Like no background check before the candidate signs consent?
Yes, and the e-signature timestamp is the evidence. Key or SOX controls need a control review.
lines.say: Yes, and the e-signature timestamp is the evidence. Key or socks controls need a control review.

params.title: Country notes for TA-05

groups.label: No criminal check before the offer

params.note: Add a country note only where local law changes a step

lines.text: Step four: country notes, only where local law changes a step.
Okay, give me a real example.
California bans criminal checks before a conditional offer. In China, private employers can't get official criminal records.
Step five: submit. The process chain ends with the Head of HR Operations.
So I refresh my inbox every four minutes?
No need. The Approvals page shows which step it's on.

params.title: Reality first, then improve it
params.next: Episode 4: Set up and run an approval chain

lines.text: Workshop, map, controls, country notes, submit. Reality first, improvements second.
And no unicorns. Next time: who actually clicks approve?

videos.title: Set up and run an approval chain
videos.summary: What an approval chain is, how editors change the defaults or build their own with named approvers, and how submitting, approving, sending back and the audit trail work.

params.title: Set up and run an approval chain
params.subtitle: Who signs, in what order, with proof

lines.text: Okay, the big question. Who actually clicks approve?
The approval chain decides. It's the route an item takes, one sign-off at a time.

steps.title: Public company and semiconductor
steps.detail: SOX, SEC, insider trading, export control

lines.text: There are five default chains: global policy, process, legal obligation, public company controls and project documents.
Wait, can I create my own approval chain?
Yes. Editors can change any default chain or build a brand new one.
Open Approvals, edit a chain or click New chain, and name each step clearly.
Then who signs each step? Can I just put Chip?
Chip has no hands. Assign named people, then choose whether any or all must sign.
So if my approver's on vacation, I add a backup and set it to any?
Exactly. Mark steps optional too, like works council consultation, and skip them with a note where not needed.
The owner clicks Submit for approval. Each approver, in turn, sees it under Waiting on you.
So this is where someone actually clicks approve.
Right here. Approve, or send it back with a reason the owner can act on.
And if Legal sends it back?
The owner fixes it and resubmits, and the chain carries on to final approval.

params.label: Audit evidence
params.text: Every approval, send-back, reason and timestamp is recorded. The audit trail is your evidence.

lines.text: Every approval, send-back and reason is time-stamped. That audit trail is your evidence.
So when auditors ask who approved it, nobody digs through email. Chip's thrilled.

params.title: Name it, staff it, run it, prove it
params.next: Episode 5: Take a policy live in 13 countries

lines.text: Put named approvers on every chain by October 30, and run one test submission end to end.
lines.say: Put named approvers on every chain by October thirtieth, and run one test submission end to end.

lines.text: Next time, a policy goes live in 13 countries. Bring snacks.

videos.title: Take a policy live in 13 countries
videos.summary: How a global policy and its country addenda clear local gates, then get published, communicated, acknowledged and evidenced in all 13 jurisdictions.

params.title: Take a policy live in 13 countries
params.subtitle: One global policy, local addenda, no surprises

lines.text: POL-09, anti-harassment, is approved. So we're done, right?
lines.say: Policy nine, anti-harassment, is approved. So we're done, right?

lines.text: Approved isn't live. Thirteen countries take a little choreography first.
Every policy is one global document plus country addenda that only cover what local law changes.
So not thirteen separate copies, each called final_v7?
lines.say: So not thirteen separate copies, each called final v seven?

lines.text: Nope. One source, with local differences marked and translated where needed.

params.title: Countries with extra gates
params.note: Plus local language versions, for example German, Chinese and Vietnamese

lines.text: Four countries add gates. In Germany, the works council co-determines conduct rules, so you need its agreement.
And China? I'm guessing an email won't cut it.
China needs democratic consultation. Vietnam registers internal labor regulations, and Taiwan files work rules with the labor authority.

bars.label: Vietnam and Taiwan: consult and file

lines.text: These gates take weeks, so plan backwards from your go-live date and start early.
And mind the calendar. Year-end freeze, then Lunar New Year and Tet from February 5 to 14.
lines.say: And mind the calendar. Year-end freeze, then Lunar New Year and Tet from February fifth to fourteenth.

lines.text: Right. Finish China, Taiwan and Vietnam before that break, or your launch slips.

steps.title: Publish
steps.detail: Policy guide updated, effective date set

steps.title: Communicate
steps.detail: Managers first, then everyone, in local languages

steps.title: Acknowledge
steps.detail: Every employee confirms they've read it

lines.text: On launch day, publish in the Policy guide with an effective date, then communicate, managers first.
Then the hard part: getting people to actually read it.
Collect acknowledgments, then file the evidence: acknowledgment reports, filings and consultation minutes.
Wait, why is Vietnam still in review?
It's waiting on the authority's receipt. Once that's attached, the gate is cleared.
So now I can set everything to Live?
Now you can: every country's evidence is filed. That's what auditors sample.
